quote: But it's gotta be a catch to it. What am I what am I eventually gonna pay? Nothing is free. So
stewart_read: This is a textbook opening for the 'what's expensive is not switching' flip, but the rep answered with mechanics (paying for panel output instead of utility) rather than inverting the framing. Also functions as a scam_anxiety_signal — the customer is pattern-matching this call to a scam.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may have judged that explaining the billing mechanism first was necessary before any reframe would land — a sequencing choice rather than a miss.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to name the suspicion directly and flip it: acknowledge 'free' sounds like a catch, then pivot to the utility's guaranteed rate increases as the actual ongoing cost.

quote: Let me just meet I don't wanna send you anything because I don't know who you are.
stewart_read: Customer is directly questioning the rep's legitimacy and the rep never restates how the lead was sourced (the form-fill mentioned at 00:08 is never re-anchored here) to rebuild trust at the exact moment it's being questioned.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may have judged the earlier form-fill mention at the open was sufficient and didn't want to re-litigate it mid-call.
coaching_implication: When a customer explicitly says 'I don't know who you are,' restate the lead source specifically (the form, the timestamp, anything concrete) — vagueness at this exact moment increases suspicion per protocol guidance.

quote: Because, I mean, there is a gentleman across from me that has, you know, that has solar. So
stewart_read: Customer is volunteering neighbor-influence as a legitimacy signal for solar in general — a warm data point that softens her skepticism — but the rep does not reflect it back or use it to build social proof.
coaching_implication: Reflect neighbor-influence back explicitly ('that's great context — a lot of folks feel more comfortable once they've seen it work next door') to reinforce the customer's own reason for openness rather than letting it pass silently.

quote: I will need a push, sir. I mean, interest, pass by natural gas
stewart_read: The bill-collection detour runs from roughly 07:04 to 12:24 — over five minutes — with the customer reading irrelevant bill fields aloud while the rep repeatedly clarifies what's needed. This matches the schema's flagged failure mode of not pivoting within the 2-minute budget.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may have judged verbal read-back was already the correct pivot (per schema) and was simply executing it slowly due to customer's own bill-navigation difficulty.
coaching_implication: Once the customer said she'd screenshot and send the usage graph (implied achievable), the rep should have moved there faster rather than continuing several more rounds of verbal back-and-forth on line items that don't matter (CCS, on-peak dollar figures, etc.).

quote: Because I'm seeing here how much are you paying? Do you know? On average?
stewart_read: The bill-amount question is asked very late — after the kWh screenshot has already been captured — reversing the schema's intended ask-then-anchor sequence, and the customer's answer ('Too much... I don't know') is never followed up with a number.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may have intentionally deprioritized the dollar figure since the kWh usage data (already captured) is what the design team actually needs, treating the dollar-bill question as a secondary courtesy ask.
coaching_implication: Ask 'how much are you paying' earlier in the call, before the technical kWh extraction, so it can be used as the emotional anchor rather than a trailing afterthought that gets a shrug answer.

quote: You're always gonna pay your utility bills. You're always gonna have Excel, and they can raise the rates anytime they want.
stewart_read: This is a genuine, schema-aligned flip — using the guaranteed-rate-increase framing to make staying with the utility the risk, not switching to solar. It's a partial success: the strategy is correctly deployed and directly precedes the customer's warmest line in the whole call ('I'm willing to listen to you guys'), but it comes nearly 13 minutes in, only after the customer had already voiced the free/catch suspicion four separate times without this reframe.
alternative_hypothesis: This could be read as a pure failure (never used the flip) but the transcript shows the rep did deploy it — the miss is timing, not absence.
coaching_implication: Credit the rep for having this move in their toolkit, but coach on deploying it in the first two minutes when the 'nothing is free' objection first surfaces rather than waiting until after the long bill-collection detour.

quote: By the twenty fifth, I still still should I should start feeling better. I can move around. Try. You might be Are you there?
stewart_read: Customer books around a real physical recovery uncertainty and hedges her own commitment with 'should' and 'try' — the rep locks the time without flagging or softening this contingency for the handoff.
coaching_implication: Flag this appointment as conditional in the handoff — the closer should know the customer's recovery timeline is a genuine risk to the sit, not just a scheduling preference.

quote: Okay. Great. When we get closer to the day, we will reach out just to confirm with you. And, yeah, just a text message so you can just respond to yes if you're still available.
stewart_read: The call ends without the verbal handshake ('is that fair?'), the one-hour block statement, or the no-driving/computer instruction — all required button-up elements are skipped in favor of a passive future-confirmation promise.
coaching_implication: Drill the full button-up sequence: time block, computer/no-driving ask, and the explicit 'is that fair?' close — all three are missing here despite a date and time being secured.
